lessons.title: Sign tests for a population median
lessons.summary: Use directions of deviations when a normal or symmetric model is not justified.
lessons.objective: Test a population median or a median paired change using exact sign probabilities.
lessons.before: Review binomial probabilities and hypotheses, significance and tails. Distinguish a population median from a mean.
lessons.ideas:
Fewer assumptions still means some assumptions

A non-parametric procedure avoids specifying a full normal model. It still needs a suitable sampling design and assumptions matching its parameter. The sign test uses independent observations from a continuous population. Under H₀: m=m₀, each observation is equally likely to fall above or below m₀; symmetry is not required.

Count above the null value

\[\begin{gathered}d_i=x_i-m_0\\B=\#\{i:d_i>0\}\\B\sim\mathrm B(n,1/2)\\(H_0).\end{gathered}\]

Here n is the number of usable observations, not the number of positive signs. This chapter’s written tasks have no exact reference equalities. If a zero occurs, the ordinary sign-test convention omits it; do not count it as positive or negative, and consider whether recording precision affects the continuous model.

For H₁: m>m₀ use P(B≥b); for m<m₀ use P(B≤b). For a two-sided test use twice the smaller inclusive tail, capped at 1. With probability 1/2 the binomial distribution is symmetric, so this can be calculated using the smaller sign count. Reject when the appropriate p-value is at most α; a tabulated rejection boundary is inclusive.

Paired sign tests concern individual changes

For matched observations define a consistent difference, such as old time minus new time. Test its population median against the stated improvement threshold. Independent pairs are required; readings within a pair need not be independent. The median of individual differences is not generally the difference of the two marginal medians.

A normal approximation has a direction

\[\begin{gathered}\mathrm E(B)=n/2\\\operatorname{Var}(B)=n/4.\end{gathered}\]

When a normal approximation is requested and suitable, include +0.5 for a lower inclusive tail and −0.5 for an upper inclusive tail. The correction approximates a discrete event by an area. Exact binomial probabilities are preferable when easily available. Do not switch between exact and approximate procedures midway through a boundary calculation.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the population median and state H₀ and H₁.
  2. Form deviations from the null, or paired changes minus the threshold.
  3. Count positive and negative signs and identify n.
  4. Calculate the correct inclusive binomial tail, doubling only for a two-sided test.
  5. Compare with α and conclude about the population parameter in context.
mistakes: A population median is not a sample median or mean.
The sign test does not require symmetry; the signed-rank test does.
For a one-sided claim use the tail in that direction.
Independent pairs do not mean that the two readings within a pair are independent.
Non-rejection does not prove the proposed median.

examples.title: 1 · A two-sided exact sign test
examples.question: Ten independent dispatch measurements are 46,52,41,49,47,43,48,42,45,44 minutes. Use a sign test at 5% for H₀: m=50 against H₁: m≠50. Assume a continuous population.
examples.solution:
Only 52 is above 50, giving b=1 and nine negative signs. Under H₀, B∼B(10,1/2).

\[p=2\,\mathrm P(B\le1)=2\frac{1+10}{2^{10}}=\frac{11}{512}.\]

This is approximately 0.0215, below 0.05. Reject H₀: there is sufficient evidence that the population median dispatch measurement differs from 50 minutes. The calculation uses signs, not the size of the largest deviation.

examples.title: 2 · An improvement must exceed the stated threshold
examples.question: Eight independent matched trials produce old-minus-new time reductions 1.8,2.1,0.7,2.5,1.6,1.3,2.8,1.1 seconds. Test whether the population median reduction exceeds 1 second at 5%. Assume continuous paired reductions.
examples.solution:
Compare each reduction with 1, not zero. Seven exceed 1 and one is below 1.

\[\begin{gathered}H_0:m_d=1\\H_1:m_d>1\\p=\mathrm P(B\ge7)=\frac{8+1}{2^8}=\frac9{256}.\end{gathered}\]

Reject at 5%. The evidence concerns the median individual reduction being greater than 1 second; it does not say every trial improves.

examples.title: 3 · An upper-tail continuity correction
examples.question: A sign test has n=40 and b=28. Use a normal approximation for H₁: m>m₀, with the supplied 5% upper critical value 1.645.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mu_B=20\\\sigma_B^2=10\\z=\frac{28-0.5-20}{\sqrt{10}}=\frac{15}{2\sqrt{10}}.\end{gathered}\]

The statistic is approximately 2.372, above 1.645. Reject in the upper direction. The subtraction of 0.5 represents the start of the inclusive event B≥28.

examples.title: 4 · A robust test does not guarantee significance
examples.question: Seven independent delay readings are 2,3,4,5,6,8,70. Symmetry is doubtful. Test the continuous population median 10 against a two-sided alternative at 5% using signs.
examples.solution:
One observation exceeds 10, so

\[p=2\,\mathrm P(\mathrm B(7,1/2)\le1)=2\frac{1+7}{128}=\frac18.\]

Do not reject at 5%. A sign test avoids a symmetry assumption, but this small sample does not provide enough evidence against the median 10. The extreme reading alone does not determine a population shape or justify a signed-rank model.

lessons.title: Signed ranks for one population
lessons.summary: Use magnitudes through their ranks, while retaining signs and the correct alternative.
lessons.objective: Calculate exact or normally approximated signed-rank tests under a continuous symmetric population model.
lessons.before: Complete sign tests. Review rank order, absolute values and normal standardisation.
lessons.ideas:
The extra information needs an extra assumption

For independent observations from a continuous population symmetric about its median, use dᵢ=xᵢ−m₀. Rank |dᵢ| from smallest to largest, then restore signs. Under the null the signs are equally likely for a given set of magnitudes. This produces the signed-rank null distribution.

\[\begin{gathered}W_+=\sum_{d_i>0}r_i\\W_-=\sum_{d_i<0}r_i\\W_++W_-=\frac{n(n+1)}2.\end{gathered}\]

The displayed formula assumes no zero deviations or tied absolute deviations, as in the supplied written tasks. Ties receive average ranks and zeros need a stated treatment; an ordinary no-ties table or variance must not then be applied without checking its applicability.

Do not fold away a one-sided direction

For a two-sided test, T=min(W₊,W₋) measures extremeness in either direction. For an increase use a large W₊ or equivalently a small W₋; for a decrease use a small W₊. A small T alone could point in the opposite direction to a one-sided claim.

Exact critical tables often give a lower-tail boundary c. For an upper alternative compare W₋ with c; for a lower alternative compare W₊ with c. A two-sided table already allows for both tails. Confirm the sample size, sidedness and significance level before comparing, and include equality in rejection.

Approximate the directional rank sum

\[\begin{gathered}\mu=\frac{n(n+1)}4\\\sigma^2=\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{24}.\end{gathered}\]

These are moments of W₊ (and of W₋), not the true moments of the folded minimum T. For a two-sided approximation, reflect to the smaller observed sum, compute its lower inclusive tail with +0.5, then double that tail. For a one-sided test use the directional W₊ with +0.5 for a lower tail or −0.5 for an upper tail.

Recovering a boundary

Rearrange the corrected normal inequality using the unrounded critical quantile. Then check both adjacent integers using the same tail rule. Rejection at p≤α means the first non-rejected value must give a p-value strictly greater than α.
lessons.method:
1. Check continuity, symmetry and independent sampling.
  2. Subtract the null median and rank absolute deviations.
  3. Calculate W₊, W₋ and their total as a check.
  4. Select the exact table or the requested normal approximation and directional tail.
  5. Apply the critical boundary or p-value and conclude about the population median.
mistakes: Rank the absolute deviations, not the observations or signed deviations.
Use the sample size after any stated zero treatment.
A small minimum is insufficient for a one-sided claim.
Use the continuity correction for the event being approximated.
Do not describe the no-ties W₊ moments as exact moments of min(W₊,W₋).

examples.title: 1 · A complete signed-rank calculation
examples.question: Six independent deviations from a proposed median are −0.6,0.2,1.1,−0.4,1.8,2.6. Assume a continuous symmetric population. Find the rank sums and exact two-sided p-value.
examples.solution:
Ranks of absolute deviations
Deviation−0.60.21.1−0.41.82.6
Rank314256
\[\begin{gathered}W_+=16\\W_-=5\\T=5\\W_++W_-=21.\end{gathered}\]

Under H₀, all 2⁶ assignments of signs to ranks 1,…,6 are equally likely. Ten produce W₊≤5; symmetry supplies the other tail.

\[p=\frac{2(10)}{64}=\frac5{16}.\]

There is insufficient evidence against the proposed median at 5%.

examples.title: 2 · A small minimum in the wrong direction
examples.question: Eight deviations from a null median are −1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8. Use an exact signed-rank test for a decrease at 5%, assuming independent continuous symmetric observations.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}W_+=35\\W_-=1\\T=1.\end{gathered}\]

A decrease requires small W₊, whereas the observed positive rank sum is almost its maximum. The appropriate lower-tail probability is

\[\mathrm P(W_+\le35)=\frac{255}{256}.\]

Do not reject in favour of a decrease. Using the small minimum 1 with a lower critical value would mistakenly count evidence of an increase as evidence of a decrease.

examples.title: 3 · Standardise a large positive rank sum
examples.question: A no-ties signed-rank test has n=20 and W₊=150. Use the normal approximation and continuity correction for an upper alternative at 5%, using 1.645.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mu=105\\\sigma^2=\frac{1435}{2}\\z=\frac{150-0.5-105}{\sqrt{1435/2}}.\end{gathered}\]

The statistic is approximately 1.661, just above 1.645, so reject in the upper direction. Using W₊ with an upper tail preserves the claim being investigated.

examples.title: 4 · Find the first non-rejected integer
examples.question: A no-ties two-sided signed-rank test has n=24 and significance level 5%. With the normal approximation and continuity correction, find the least possible T=min(W₊,W₋) that does not reject.
examples.solution:
The directional rank-sum moments are μ=150 and σ²=1225, so σ=35. The lower reflected rejection boundary satisfies

\[T\le150-0.5-1.959964(35)\approx80.9013.\]

Thus the least non-rejected integer is 81. At T=80 the corrected z is −69.5/35≈−1.986 and the two-sided p-value is below 0.05. At T=81 it is −68.5/35≈−1.957 and the p-value is above 0.05.

lessons.title: Matched pairs and ranked changes
lessons.summary: Preserve the pairing, the units and the parameter being tested.
lessons.objective: Use signed ranks for individual paired changes and assess the effect of recording corrections.
lessons.before: Complete signed ranks and paired sign tests. Review subtraction and unit conversion.
lessons.ideas:
One sample of changes

A matched-pairs signed-rank test applies the one-sample procedure to differences from meaningful pairs. Examples include the same object measured twice, or matched units with random allocation. Different pairs must be independent; the population of paired differences must be continuous and symmetric about its median. Normality is not required.

\[\begin{gathered}D_i=A_i-B_i\\d_i=D_i-\delta_0.\end{gathered}\]

Choose the direction so that a positive D has a clear interpretation. To test whether the median improvement exceeds δ₀, rank |Dᵢ−δ₀|, not |Dᵢ|. The parameter is the median of the individual differences, not generally the difference of the two population medians.

Independence and randomised order

The observations within a pair are related by design. Order or practice effects can be confounded with a treatment if everyone uses the same method first. Randomised order and independent pairs help support the comparison, but a statistical rejection does not automatically establish that every individual benefits.

Corrections may change signs or ranks

At a zero null, swapping the two readings of one pair reverses its difference without changing the absolute value. Its rank moves from one sign sum to the other; no reranking is needed. If a magnitude changes, all affected ranks must be recalculated. With a non-zero null, even swapping readings can change |D−δ₀|, so the zero-null shortcut need not work.

Adding or subtracting the same amount from both readings in a pair leaves D unchanged. Convert both readings to the same units before forming differences. Multiplying every difference and the null threshold by the same positive factor preserves signs and ranks; changing just one side’s units does not.

Choose sign, signed-rank or t appropriately

A sign test can test a continuous median difference without symmetry. Signed-rank uses more order information but adds symmetry. A paired t-test concerns a mean difference and, for a small sample, needs a justified normal-difference model. Different procedures and parameters need not give identical decisions.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the matching and make the units consistent.
  2. Define D=A−B and the null median difference δ₀.
  3. Rank |D−δ₀|, preserving signs separately.
  4. Calculate directional rank sums and apply the correct tail.
  5. For corrections, decide whether only a sign changes or whether reranking is necessary.
mistakes: Equal sample sizes do not create matched pairs.
Subtract the proposed median change before ranking.
The symmetry assumption concerns paired differences.
A sign-only correction shortcut needs unchanged absolute deviations.
An average or median change does not imply every individual improves.

examples.solution:
The before-minus-after differences are (0.3,1.1,−0.6,1.8,0.2,2.6), with ranks (2,4,3,5,1,6).

\[\begin{gathered}W_+=18\\W_-=3\\p=\mathrm P(W_+\ge18)=\frac5{64}.\end{gathered}\]

examples.title: 2 · Improvement above two units
examples.question: Eight independent paired reductions are 2.4,3.6,1.1,5.2,4.3,2.8,6.1,0.7. Under a continuous symmetric difference model, test whether their population median exceeds 2 at 5%. The supplied one-sided lower critical rank sum is 5.
examples.solution:
Subtract 2 first: (0.4,1.6,−0.9,3.2,2.3,0.8,4.1,−1.3). Their absolute ranks are (1,5,3,7,6,2,8,4).

\[\begin{gathered}W_+=29\\W_-=7.\end{gathered}\]

The upper alternative uses the small negative rank sum. Since 7>5, do not reject. Ranking the unadjusted reductions would test a different null.

examples.title: 3 · A transposed pair reaches a critical boundary
examples.question: For eight independent symmetric paired differences, the zero-null differences are (1,−2,3,4,−5,6,7,8). A positive median change is tested using the supplied lower critical value 5. The second pair was transposed. Correct it without unnecessary reranking.
examples.solution:
Initially W₊=29 and W₋=7, so the upper alternative does not reject. Transposing the second pair changes −2 to +2; its absolute rank stays 2.

\[\begin{gathered}W_+^{\mathrm{new}}=31\\W_-^{\mathrm{new}}=5.\end{gathered}\]

The corrected result rejects, including equality at the critical boundary. This shortcut is justified by the zero null and unchanged magnitudes.

examples.title: 4 · Convert the readings before subtracting
examples.question: Before times in minutes are (4.5,5.3,3.8,6.1,4.9); the paired after times in seconds are (258,282,234,348,264). Find the before-minus-after signed-rank sums for a zero null.
examples.solution:
Dividing the after readings by 60 gives (4.3,4.7,3.9,5.8,4.4). Differences in minutes are (0.2,0.6,−0.1,0.3,0.5), with ranks (2,5,1,3,4).

\[\begin{gathered}W_+=14\\W_-=1\\W_++W_-=15.\end{gathered}\]

Subtracting seconds directly from minutes would rank meaningless differences. If both readings in a pair were 6 seconds too high, correcting both would leave that pair’s difference unchanged.

lessons.title: Rank-sum tests for independent groups
lessons.summary: Rank both samples together and distinguish rank sums from signed ranks.
lessons.objective: Test a common-shape location comparison with exact or approximate rank-sum methods.
lessons.before: Review matched versus independent designs, combined ranking and normal tails.
lessons.ideas:
Independent groups are not artificial pairs

Rank all observations from both groups together from smallest to largest, retaining their group labels. Under the null of the same continuous distribution, the allocations of group labels to ranks are equally likely. The rank-sum procedure is different from ranking within-pair deviations.

For the 9231 interpretation as a comparison of population medians, use independent continuous populations that are symmetric with the same shape and spread, differing at most by location. A rank-sum rejection for general unequal shapes cannot automatically be described as a difference of medians.

Keep the sample identity in the statistic

Let m≤n and let R be the ascending rank sum for the smaller sample. Reversing the rank direction changes each rank r to m+n+1−r, so that sample’s reversed rank sum is

\[\begin{gathered}R^*=m(m+n+1)-R\\W=\min(R,R^*).\end{gathered}\]

This MF19 reflected statistic is not generally min(RA,RB) when sample sizes differ. The two ordinary sample rank sums instead total (m+n)(m+n+1)/2. With equal sizes either group can be designated; state which one is used.

Direction still matters

With ascending ranks, larger observations in group A give a larger RA. For a one-sided alternative use the correct directional tail; the folded W alone discards that direction. Exact tables give a lower-tail critical boundary for the specified sample sizes and significance level.

Normal approximation without ties

\[\begin{gathered}\mu_R=\frac{m(m+n+1)}2\\\sigma_R^2=\frac{mn(m+n+1)}{12}.\end{gathered}\]

These are moments of the directional R, not the true moments of its folded minimum. Use −0.5 for an inclusive upper tail and +0.5 for an inclusive lower tail. For a two-sided calculation reflect to the smaller same-sample rank sum and double its lower tail. No-ties formulas and tables need adjustment if tied measurements occur.

Boundary questions require checking the neighbouring attainable integer rank sums. A common-shape median comparison and a normal equal-variance mean comparison use different information; even when both models are justified their test decisions need not coincide.
lessons.method:
1. Check independence, continuity and the common-shape location model for a median interpretation.
  2. Rank the combined observations and sum ranks by group.
  3. Identify the smaller sample and its reflected rank sum, checking the total.
  4. Use the exact table or requested normal approximation with the directional alternative.
  5. Conclude in context, keeping median, mean and distributional claims distinct.
mistakes: Do not rank each independent sample separately.
The MF19 reflection is of the same sample’s rank sum.
Do not replace the reflection by the other group’s rank sum for unequal sizes.
Equal sample sizes are not evidence of matching.
A median interpretation needs the stated common-shape model.

examples.title: 1 · Unequal sizes expose the wrong minimum
examples.question: Independent groups give A=(12,14,17,18) and B=(11,13,15,16,19). Rank the nine measurements together and calculate RA, RB and the MF19 statistic.
examples.solution:
A receives ranks (2,4,7,8), so RA=21. B receives (1,3,5,6,9), so RB=24. Their total is 45. The smaller sample has m=4 and n=5.

\[\begin{gathered}R_A^*=4(10)-21=19\\W=\min(21,19)=19.\end{gathered}\]

Using min(21,24)=21 would give the wrong MF19 statistic.

examples.title: 2 · An exact directional rank test
examples.question: Independent groups give A=(8,10,12,14) and B=(1,2,3,4,6). Under a continuous symmetric common-shape location model, test whether A has the greater population median at 5%.
examples.solution:
The A ranks are (6,7,8,9), giving RA=30, its largest possible value. Under the null there are C(9,4)=126 equally likely assignments of four ranks to A. Only one has sum at least 30.

\[p=\mathrm P(R_A\ge30)=\frac1{126}.\]

Reject in the upper direction at 5%. This is a population location comparison under the stated model, not a claim about every future pair of observations.

examples.title: 3 · A normal approximation to an ascending rank sum
examples.question: Independent no-ties samples have sizes m=12 and n=15. The ascending rank sum for A, the smaller group, is 220. Test an upper location alternative using the supplied normal critical value 1.645.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\mu_R=168\\\sigma_R^2=420\\z=\frac{220-0.5-168}{\sqrt{420}}.\end{gathered}\]

The statistic is approximately 2.513, above 1.645. Under the stated continuous symmetric common-shape location model, this gives evidence of a greater population median in A at 5%. The −0.5 correction is for RA≥220.

examples.title: 4 · The least rejecting rank sum
examples.question: Independent no-ties samples have sizes m=10 and n=12. Find the least integer ascending rank sum for the smaller sample that rejects in favour of a greater population location at 5%, using the normal approximation with continuity correction.
examples.solution:
Here μ=115 and σ²=230. Upper-tail rejection requires

\[\frac{R-0.5-115}{\sqrt{230}}\ge1.644854.\]

The real boundary is approximately 140.445. Therefore the least rejecting integer is 141. At 140 the corrected statistic is below the critical value; at 141 it is above. These are attainable rank sums for the sample sizes.

questions.prompt_html:
A parcel distributor states that the population median delay between booking and dispatch is 24 hours. An independent random sample of 17 bookings gives the following delays, in hours.

Observed values

questions.answer_html:
(a)

The exceptionally long delays suggest a right-skewed population; symmetry is doubtful.

(b)

\(B=4,\ n=17,\ p=0.049042\). There is sufficient evidence at the 10% significance level to conclude that the population median delay differs from 24 hours.

(a)

Most recorded delays lie below 30 hours, but one is 132.5 hours. This suggests a long right tail, so a population distribution symmetric about its median is doubtful. A sign test does not require symmetry. A sample cannot by itself prove that the population is skewed.

Let \(m\) be the population median delay in hours.

\[H_0:m=24,\qquad H_1:m\ne24.\]

\[B=\text{number of positive signs},\qquad B\sim\operatorname{Bin}(17,\tfrac12)\quad(H_0).\]
\[p=2\mathrm P(B\le 4)=2\sum_{j=0}^{4}\binom{17}{j}2^{-17}=0.049042.\]

The p-value is no greater than \(0.1\), so reject \(H_0\).

A validated historical standard specifies a population median seal-breaking force of 44 N. This value is treated as known, not estimated from the sample below. After a process change, 26 packages are sampled independently; their breaking forces, in newtons, are recorded.

questions.prompt_html:
Eleven independently sampled insulating strips have the following lengths, in millimetres. The production target is a population median of 120 mm.

Observed values

Assume that the relevant population distribution is continuous and symmetric about its median. No normality assumption is made.

  1. Carry out a sign test at the 10% level.

    [4]

  2. Carry out a Wilcoxon signed-rank test at the same level and compare the decision with part (a).

    [4]

  3. Do the two decisions establish that the population median is exactly 120 mm? Explain briefly.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(B=8,\ n=11,\ p=0.226562\). There is insufficient evidence at the 10% significance level to conclude that the population median strip length differs from 120 mm.

(b)

\(W_+=45,\ W_-=21\), critical value \(13\). There is insufficient evidence at the 10% significance level to conclude that the population median strip length differs from 120 mm.

questions.title: A large-sample rank-sum summary
questions.prompt_html:
Independent random samples contain 80 response times from service system A and 95 from system B. All 175 observations are ranked together from shortest (rank 1) to longest (rank 175), without ties. The sum of the ranks for system A is 6335. A comparison of the population median response times is required.

  1. Use a Wilcoxon rank-sum test with a normal approximation and continuity correction, at the 5% level, to investigate a difference in the population medians.

    [6]

  2. State a population-shape assumption needed for this median comparison in the 9231 model.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(R_A=6335,\ W=6335\), \(z=-2.110\). There is sufficient evidence at the 5% significance level to conclude that the population median response times differ between the two service systems.

(b)

The populations are symmetric with the same shape and spread, differing at most by location.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(m_A\) and \(m_B\) denote the population medians. For this median comparison, use a symmetric, common-shape location model: equality of medians then corresponds to identical population distributions.

\[H_0:m_A=m_B,\qquad H_1:m_A\nem_B.\]

The sample sizes are \(m=80,\ n=95\), with A chosen as the sample of size \(m\).

\[W=\min\left(R_A,\ m(m+n+1)-R_A\right)=\min(6335,7745)=6335.\]

For unequal sample sizes, the reflected rank sum \(m(m+n+1)-R_A\) is not the rank sum \(R_B\) of the other sample.

Use the prescribed normal approximation to \(R_A\). Under the null hypothesis:

\[\mu_R=\frac{m(m+n+1)}{2}=7040,\qquad \sigma_R^2=\frac{mn(m+n+1)}{12}=111466.666667.\]

Use the smaller reflected tail \(R_A\le 6335\) and double its probability. The normal distribution approximates the rank sum, not the minimum \(W\) as a separate random variable.

\[z=\frac{6335+0.5-7040}{\sqrt{111466.666667}}=-2.110126.\]

The relevant normal critical value is \(-1.960\). The approximate two-sided p-value is \(0.034847\).

Thus reject \(H_0\) at the 5% level.

Conclusion. There is sufficient evidence at the 5% significance level to conclude that the population median response times differ between the two service systems.

(b)

For the stated median interpretation, use symmetric population distributions of common shape and spread, with a possible location shift. Random sampling and independence are already given. A difference in rank distributions should not automatically be interpreted as only a difference in medians when shapes differ.

(a)

Rank the combined samples, not each sample separately. For unequal sample sizes use the reflected rank sum, not the other sample sum.

(b)

The test is intended to compare location rather than a change in shape.
